title: Sharp Empirical Bernstein Inequalities for the Variance of Bounded Random Variables
claim: Our proposed confidence interval is much tighter than the standard baseline across sample sizes and distributions, converging to the true value.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, shared legend style, bands around curves
description: Three side-by-side line plots, labeled (I), (II) and (III), one for each data distribution (uniform, Beta(2,6) and Beta(5,5)). Each plot has sample size from 0 to 5000 on the x-axis and estimated standard deviation on the y-axis. Blue curves show the baseline MP upper and lower confidence bounds. Orange curves show the proposed EB bounds. A purple dashed horizontal line marks the true std. Shaded bands show the empirical quantiles around each curve. Both sets of bounds start wide and narrow as the sample size grows. The orange EB curves sit visibly closer to the true std line than the blue MP curves, with a smaller gap at every sample size. In panels II and III the lower bounds are clipped at zero for small samples. A legend in the top right of each panel names the three lines.
caption: Average confidence intervals over $100$ simulations for the std $\sigma$ for (I) the uniform distribution in $(0,1)$, (II) the beta distribution with parameters $(2, 6)$, and (III) the beta distribution with parameters $(5, 5)$. For each of the inequalities, the $0.95%$-empirical quantiles are also displayed. The Maurer Pontil (MP) inequality [ref] is compared against our proposal (EB). We highlight the improved empirical performance of our methods in all scenarios.
abstract: We develop novel empirical Bernstein inequalities for the variance of bounded random variables. Our inequalities hold under constant conditional variance and mean, without further assumptions like independence or identical distribution of the random variables, making them suitable for sequential decision making contexts. The results are instantiated for both the batch setting (where the sample size is fixed) and the sequential setting (where the sample size is a stopping time). Our bounds are asymptotically sharp: when the data are iid, our CI adpats optimally to both unknown mean $Î¼$ and unknown $\mathbb{V}[(X-Î¼)^2]$, meaning that the first order term of our CI exactly matches that of the oracle Bernstein inequality which knows those quantities. We compare our results to a widely used (non-sharp) concentration inequality for the variance based on self-bounding random variables, showing both the theoretical gains and improved empirical performance of our approach. We finally extend our methods to work in any separable Hilbert space.
